findings.title: KeyError/500 when existing Integration has no 'sender' in metadata
findings.body: GitHubInstallation.dispatch accesses `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` unconditionally when an Integration exists but no OrganizationIntegration does. However, `build_integration` only stores `metadata["sender"]` when `state.get("sender")` is set, so Integrations can legitimately exist without a "sender" key (e.g. created through the pipeline when the installation webhook never supplied a sender, or legacy rows). For such installations this line raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of a graceful error page. The lookup should use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and treat a missing sender as a failed verification.

findings.title: Installer verification is skipped when the installation webhook has not yet created the Integration
findings.body: The new user-identity check (comparing `github_authenticated_user` against `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`) only runs on the branch where the Integration row already exists. That row is created by the GitHub `installation` webhook; if the webhook is delayed or lost, `Integration.objects.get` raises DoesNotExist and dispatch calls `pipeline.next_step()` with no verification at all, and `build_integration` later creates the Integration without a sender. This means the security control this PR is meant to add can be bypassed by simply racing the webhook (or by webhook delivery failure), which is a common condition in practice. The verification (or an explicit 'installation not yet registered, retry' failure) should also apply on the DoesNotExist path, or the pipeline should wait/retry until the webhook-created Integration is visible.

findings.title: OAuth 'state' is a static per-provider value, so the CSRF/state check provides no real protection
findings.body: OAuthLoginView uses `pipeline.signature` as the OAuth2 `state` and validates the callback with `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`. `Pipeline.signature` is a deterministic value derived from the pipeline/provider name (the tests hard-code the same state, `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`, across different users, organizations, and sessions), so it is identical for every user of the deployment. Any user who starts their own GitHub install flow sees this value in the authorize redirect URL and can therefore forge a valid callback for any other user's pipeline. Concretely: an attacker obtains their own OAuth `code` (authenticating as themselves), then gets a victim's browser to hit the setup URL with that code plus the known state; the token exchange succeeds in the victim's pipeline and binds the attacker's GitHub login as `github_authenticated_user`, after which the installer-identity check passes and the integration is linked. The state must be a per-pipeline/per-session random nonce (stored in pipeline state and compared on callback), not a shared constant, for the check described in the PR description to be meaningful.

findings.title: Unhandled exceptions from get_user_info and token exchange produce a 500 instead of the error page
findings.body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` is not wrapped in error handling. `get_user_info` performs an HTTP call to GitHub's /user endpoint and raises ApiError on any non-2xx response (e.g. revoked token, GitHub 5xx, secondary rate limit); `safe_urlopen` for the token exchange can likewise raise on connection errors. These exceptions propagate out of the pipeline view and result in an unhandled 500 error rather than the intended `github-integration-failed.html` error page shown for the other failure modes. The calls should be inside the try/except (or a separate one) that falls back to `error(request, self.active_organization)`.

findings.title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 404 / 'installation could not be found' path
findings.body: The test previously asserted `b"The GitHub installation could not be found."`, i.e. that build_integration's IntegrationError on a GitHub 404 is surfaced. After the change it asserts `b"Invalid installation request."` because the second request uses a state (`ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`) that does not match the pipeline signature, so the flow fails at the state check and the `responses.replace(..., status=404)` stub for `/app/installations/<id>` is never exercised. The renamed test now effectively duplicates a state-mismatch test, and the 'installation could not be found' regression path (IntegrationError raised in build_integration on GitHub 404) has no coverage. A separate test with a valid state and a 404 stub should be added, along with a dedicated test for the state-mismatch case.
